overview.text: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669) was a Dutch painter and printmaker whose portraits, history paintings, and prints helped define seventeenth-century Dutch art. Born in Leiden, he trained there and in Amsterdam before moving to Amsterdam around 1632, where he built a successful workshop. Viewers often recognize his work by its dramatic contrasts of light and dark, expressive faces and gestures, and willingness to vary composition and brushwork. His 1642 group portrait, The Night Watch, turns a civic militia portrait into an energetic scene, with figures caught in different actions rather than arranged as a still lineup. He also made technically inventive etchings and drypoints, revising plates to create different effects.

key_facts.text: Rembrandt was born in Leiden in 1606 and died in Amsterdam in 1669.
He trained with Jacob van Swanenburgh in Leiden and Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam; by 1628 he was teaching pupils.
The Night Watch was completed in 1642. Its original title is unknown; the familiar title first appeared in a document in 1797.
The Rijksmuseum describes The Night Watch as a lively group portrait: instead of posing the militia in a static lineup, Rembrandt shows its members in action.
Rembrandt made about 300 etchings and drypoints between roughly 1626 and 1665, experimenting with printing methods and sometimes substantially reworking plates.
